Kabeiria: a city in western Asia, whose land the Kabeiroi used to
inhabit. There are also Kabeiroi, a people in Boiotia, as per
Pausanias, book 9. Kabeiria is also 'Kabeiros', from which comes
the forms 'Kabeiraios', 'Kabeiraia' and 'Kabeirites'. As for the
Kabeirion, the ethnonym of this is 'Kabeirios' (as 'Byzantios' is
from the form 'Byzantion'), and the feminine is 'Kabeiria'. Also
'Kabeirieus'. As for the nymphs, 'Kabeirides' is from Kabeiro
daughter of Proteus and Anchinoe, from whom also came
Kadmilos son of Hephaistos. There are also both 'Kabeiris'
derived from the form 'Kabeiros', and 'Kabeirias' derived from the
form 'Kabeirios'. The possessives are 'Kabeirikos' and 'Kabeirike',
and 'kabeiriazesthai' is a verb.

Κάδμιλος. ἔστι δὲ ἡ μὲν Καβειρίς παρὰ τὸ Κάβειρος, ἡ
δὲ Καβειριάς παρὰ τὸ Καβείριος. τὸ κτητικὸν
Καβειρικός καὶ Καβειρική, καὶ καβειριάζεσθαι ῥῆμα.

elevation.

subsequent clarification that there was also a
people of Boeotia called Καβείριοι.

not the usual -οι (this masc. form in *-ιος has
escaped the notice of all major lexica).

Kapetolion: in Rome, a hill that was long ago called 'Tarpaios'.
Regarding the spelling of the sanctuary name, Eudaimon says
that it is with ι: 'Eirenaios accents it with acute on the antepenult
and writes it with ι.' Herodian has 'Kapetolieion' with six syllables,
and 'Kapetolion' with contraction. The form 'Kapetoleia', referring
to the games, is accented with circumflex on the penult. This is
because forms whose base already ends in postvocalic -ος—
when either a single ι is in the penultimate position or α precedes
it so that the diphthong αι stands before the ultima—will be
accented with a circumflex on the penult, and the same applies to
possessive forms. Asklepieion (Ἀσκληπιεῖον) is thus from
'Asklepios' (Ἀσκληπιός); Ptolemaeion (Πτολεμαεῖον) is thus from
'Ptolemaios' (Πτολεμαῖος); Olympieia (Ὀλυμπιεῖα), the one at
Athens, is thus from 'Olympios' (Ὀλύμπιος). The sanctuary,
however, is 'Kapetolion' (Καπετώλιον), and 'Zeus Kapetolios'
(Καπετώλιος), with ι. The ethnonym is 'Kapetolinos'.

Kappadokia: a region bordering Kilikia, as Menippos says: 'from
Sinope to the River Euarchos, which forms the border between
Paphlagonia and Kappadokia…'. The ethnonym is 'Kappadox' and
'Kappadokos'; also 'Kappadokes', as Herodotos says. The founder,
Kappadokos, is mentioned by Menander. 'Kappadokissa' is also
said, like 'Aithiopissa' and 'pandokissa'. Previously it was not
divided, as now, into 'First' and 'Second', but into 'Greater' and
'Lesser', and 'Small' and 'Big'.

final_english_translation:
Karia: the country. The ethnonym is 'Kar', homonymous with the
founder. According to the grammatical rule the feminine is ['Kaira',
also with hiatus] 'Kaïra'. The common usage, however, is with the
diphthong ει. Apollonios says that it is with long ι, as per book 5
of his *On Modifications of Forms* and in his *On Genders*. The
lengthening is necessary because of the penult, for words ending
in short α when modified in form lengthen their penult either by
nature or by position. While Herodian says that this is doubtful in
his *Orthography* (and in his *General Prosody* he says that it
uses the diphthong following the common usage), he does say
when commenting on Apollonios’ *On Genders* that it is with long
ι: 'for there is occasion when lengthening occurs after diaresis:
'oïomai' (ὀίομαι), 'oïgon' (ὄιγον), 'oïda' (ὄιδα) among the Aiolians
rather than 'oida' (οἶδα). The common usage, however, is with the
diphthong, according to the analogy of 'soteira', 'oleteira'.'
'Karios' is also said, for Zeus is honoured in this way among the
Mylasians. The feminine is 'Karia'. The acropolis of Megara also
used to be called Karia, after Kar, son of Phoroneus, and an
inhabitant is a 'Karios'. There is also 'Karine'. There is also
'Kariates'. There is also 'Kariatis' as well as 'Karis', from the
genitive of Kar. Kos also used to be called 'Karis', as per
Hellanikos. There is also a city in Phrygia: 'Karis' and 'Karides'.
The ethnonym is 'Karideus' (as in 'Arkideus'); the form according
to the grammatical rule is 'Karites'. The possessive for the
Karians is 'Karikos'. Herodotos in book 1: 'The Karikos people are
most esteemed.'

διὰ τοῦ « ι » φησὶ μακροῦ, ὡς ἐν τῷ εʹ περὶ παθῶν καὶ
ἐν τῷ περὶ γενῶν. ἡ δὲ ἔκτασις ἀναγκαία διὰ τὴν

Karpasia: a city in Cyprus, which Pygmalion founded, as per
Hellanikos in his *Kypriaka*. Dionysios, however, says it is
'Krapaseia', with a diphthong, in book 3 of his *Bassarika*: 'and
behold those [who live in] Kinyreion and steep Krapaseia'. There is
also a Karpasia island, opposite the Sarpedonian promontory, but
Xenagoras says that it is 'Karpathos'. Demetrios of Salamis says
it is 'Karbasia', because it seems to be situated facing the wind
called 'Karbas'. A citizen is a 'Karpaseotes', as in 'Mareotes'. The
possessive is 'Karpaseotikos', and there is also a 'Karpaseotic'
promontory. Theopompos calls them 'Karpaseis' in book 10,
perhaps from Karpasos (as 'Antiocheus' is from Antiochos), after
whom is 'Karpaseia'.

διφθόγγου Κραπάσειαν αὐτήν φησιν ἐν τρίτῳ
Βασσαρικῶν “ἠδ´ ὁπόσοι Κινύρειον ἰδ´ αἰπεινὴν
Κραπάσειαν”. ἔστι καὶ νῆσος Καρπασία κατὰ τὴν ἄκραν

τὸν καλούμενον κάρβαν ἄνεμον κεῖσθαι δοκεῖ. ὁ
πολίτης Καρπασεώτης ὡς Μαρεώτης. καὶ τὸ κτητικὸν
Καρπασεωτικός καὶ Καρπασεωτικὴ ἄκρα. Θεόπομπος
ἐν δεκάτῳ Καρπασεῖς αὐτούς φησιν, ἴσως ἀπὸ τοῦ
Κάρπασος, ὡς Ἀντίοχος Ἀντιοχεύς, ἀφ´ οὗ Καρπάσεια.

Karystos: a city beneath Mount Oche in Euboia. After Karystos,
son of Cheiron. Theodoridas says that it is 'Cheironia'. The city is
situated near the Myrtoan Sea beneath Mount Oche. The
mountain was named [after the mating that occurs there, either]
from the intercourse of the gods Zeus and Hera, or because
sheep conceive there when they copulate. For the Achaians say
'oche' for fodder. 'Oches' is also said in the masculine. In this city
there is 'a stone that is carded and woven, so that the woven
products are made into towels; when soiled they are thrown into
the fire and they are cleansed of their dirt, in a manner similar to
washing'. It used to be named 'Aigaia' after Aigaion who ruled
there, from whom is also the Aegean Sea. There is also a place
called Karystos in Aigys towards Arkadia, from which Alkman
says Karystion wine comes, according to Strabo, book 10. The
ethnonym of the former is 'Karystios': 'in which is the quarry of the
Karystian columns'. The feminine is 'Karystia'.
